prompt: What makes a Go package build into a program you can run, rather than a library?
hint: Look at the first line after the comment, and the function.

choices.text: Its file is called `main.go`
choices.why: File names mean nothing to the compiler here: `hello.go` built a program.

choices.text: It is `package main` and declares `func main`
choices.why: Right. The package name `main` and a function `main` in it are the whole requirement.

choices.text: It has a `go.mod` file at its root that names the module
choices.why: A library has a `go.mod` too; the module says what the code is called, not whether it runs.

choices.text: It imports the `fmt` package
choices.why: A program need not print anything, and libraries import `fmt` all the time.

prompt: `hello.go` calls `fmt.Println`. What does the capital P tell you?
hint: It is about who may call it.

choices.text: That `Println` returns values
choices.why: It does return two, but the capital has nothing to do with that.

choices.text: That `Println` is built into the language
choices.why: The built-ins, like `len`, are lower case; `Println` is an ordinary function in the `fmt` package.

choices.text: That another package is allowed to call it
choices.why: Right. A name that starts with a capital letter is exported; lesson 39 is about that rule.

choices.text: Nothing: Go capitalises every function name by convention
choices.why: `main` is a function and is lower case. The capital is a rule with an effect, not a style.

prompt: A directory becomes a module when it has a file called `___` at its root.
hint: `go mod init` writes it.

prompt: `go mod init example.com/hello` wrote `go 1.27.1` into `go.mod`. What does that line record?
hint: Where did the number come from?

choices.text: The version of the hello program
choices.why: A module's own versions are git tags, which lesson 40 covers; this line is about the language.

choices.text: The Go release installed on every machine that will ever import this module
choices.why: It cannot know that. It records what this module expects, not what others have.

choices.text: The language version the module expects, from the toolchain that ran it
choices.why: Right. The lab runs go1.27.1, so that is what `go mod init` wrote.

choices.text: The release of the server at example.com
choices.why: `example.com` is a domain reserved for examples; nothing answers there and nothing is asked.

prompt: Which of these are true of the first line of `hello.go`, `// Command hello prints a greeting.`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 04 printed it.

choices.text: `go doc` prints it as the package's documentation
choices.why: Yes: run with no argument in `~/hello`, `go doc` printed exactly this sentence.

choices.text: The program prints it when it starts
choices.why: A comment is not code; the program printed `Hello, Go` and nothing else.

choices.text: It documents the package because it sits directly above `package main`
choices.why: Yes. A comment directly above a declaration is that declaration's documentation.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a program without it
choices.why: Nothing requires it. It is a convention the tools read, not a rule the compiler enforces.

prompt: After `go run .`, what is left in the current directory?
hint: Where did the binary go?

choices.text: A binary named after the module
choices.why: That is `go build`. `go run` keeps the binary out of your directory.

choices.text: Nothing new: the binary is kept in the build cache
choices.why: Right. It compiles, runs, and keeps the result where the go command manages it.

choices.text: Nothing, because `go run` interprets the source without compiling it
choices.why: Go has no interpreter. `go run` compiles, which is why the first run after emptying the cache took seconds.

choices.text: An object file for each package it compiled
choices.why: Compiled packages go to the build cache too, never into the source directory.

prompt: After `go clean -cache`, the first `go run .` took 4.493 s and the second 0.044 s. About how many times faster was the second? Give a whole number.
hint: Divide the first by the second.

prompt: Match each command to where the binary it compiles ends up.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

prompt: You build a program like `hello` with `go build` on a Linux amd64 laptop and copy the binary to a fresh Linux amd64 server that has never had Go installed. What happens when you run it there?
hint: What did `file` say about how it was linked?

choices.text: It fails until Go is installed, because the runtime lives in `/usr/local/go`
choices.why: `/usr/local/go` is the compiler and its tools. The runtime was copied into the binary when it was built.

choices.text: It must be recompiled on the server first
choices.why: Same operating system, same architecture: there is nothing to recompile for.

choices.text: It runs: the runtime is inside the binary, and it asks the machine for a kernel
choices.why: Right. `statically linked` is the point of those 2.3 MB.

choices.text: It runs only if the server has the same C library version as the laptop
choices.why: That is the dependency a dynamically linked C program has. This binary was statically linked.

prompt: Why did the second `go run .` take 44 milliseconds when the first took four and a half seconds?
hint: What did `go clean -cache` empty?

choices.text: Nothing had changed, so the build cache already held the compiled program
choices.why: Right. The first run compiled the standard library packages too; the second reused all of it.

choices.text: The first run was downloading Go
choices.why: Go was already installed; `GOTOOLCHAIN=local` stops the lab from downloading one.

choices.text: The second run interpreted the source instead of compiling it
choices.why: There is no interpreter to fall back to. The second run used the compiled result.

choices.text: The operating system kept the first process in memory and resumed it
choices.why: The first process had ended. A new one ran the same cached binary.

prompt: Where does `go doc` get the text it prints?
hint: It worked with no network.

choices.text: From pkg.go.dev, downloaded each time
choices.why: The lab answered with no network. The website is generated from the same comments, but `go doc` does not ask it.

choices.text: From manual pages installed beside the compiler
choices.why: There are no separate manual pages; the documentation is the source's own comments.

choices.text: From comments in the source on your machine
choices.why: Right. The toolchain carries the standard library's source, comments included.

choices.text: From a documentation file that each package ships beside its code
choices.why: There is no second file to keep in step: the comment is the documentation.

prompt: A program splits the string `" go is fun"` (it starts with a space) into words. According to `go doc strings.Fields`, what does `strings.Fields` return?
hint: Read the last sentence of its documentation.

choices.text: An empty first word, then `go`, `is` and `fun`
choices.why: That is what splitting on single spaces does. `Fields` discards leading white space.

choices.text: `go`, `is` and `fun`
choices.why: Right: every element is non-empty, and leading runs of white space are discarded.

choices.text: The whole string, because it splits only on newlines
choices.why: It splits on any white space, as `unicode.IsSpace` defines it.

choices.text: An error, because the string starts with a separator
choices.why: Its signature returns `[]string` and nothing else, so it has no way to report an error.

prompt: `go doc fmt.Println` printed the signature `func Println(a ...any) (n int, err ___)`.
hint: The type that says whether writing failed.

prompt: Your project is held on an older Go release while the newest one adds a function you read about on pkg.go.dev. Which source tells you whether the Go you are running has it?
hint: Which one reads the standard library you installed?

choices.text: pkg.go.dev, because it is generated from the same comments
choices.why: Same comments, different release: the site shows the standard library of the latest Go.

choices.text: `go doc` in your terminal
choices.why: Right. It reads the source of the toolchain you are running, so it answers for that release.

choices.text: The newest release's notes, which list every addition
choices.why: They say when it arrived, not whether your installed Go has it; you would still need to know which you run.

choices.text: Any search engine, which returns the most popular page
choices.why: Popularity says nothing about which release a page describes.

prompt: What can you configure about the layout `gofmt` writes?
hint: The section lists three things people expect to set.

choices.text: The width of an indent, counted in spaces
choices.why: The indent is a tab, always.

choices.text: Where the opening brace of a block goes
choices.why: The brace goes on the same line, always; a brace on its own line does not even compile.

choices.text: The longest a line may be before it is wrapped
choices.why: There is no line length setting either.

choices.text: Nothing: it has no layout settings
choices.why: Right. That is the design, so a diff shows changes and never somebody's editor settings.

prompt: `go run .` printed `Hello, %!d(string=Ana)`. What happened?
hint: Who wrote `%!d`?

choices.text: The compiler rejected the format string and printed its error
choices.why: The program compiled and ran; that line is its output.

choices.text: `%d` was handed a string, and `fmt` wrote the mismatch into the output
choices.why: Right: `%!d(string=Ana)` names the verb and what it received.

choices.text: `Printf` converted the name to a number and overflowed
choices.why: Go converts nothing on your behalf, and certainly not a name into a number.

choices.text: The program panicked and this is the panic message
choices.why: A panic stops the program with a stack trace; this program ended normally.

prompt: Put the three commands in the order the section suggests running them before you show a Go file to anyone.
hint: Layout first.

prompt: The compiler said `./main.go:5:2: "os" imported and not used`. What is `5:2`?
hint: The file has one import block.

choices.text: Error number 5, severity 2
choices.why: Go's compiler messages carry no error numbers; this is a position.

choices.text: The fifth import, in the second file
choices.why: There is one file and two imports; the numbers point into `main.go`.

choices.text: Line 5, column 2
choices.why: Right: the second character of line 5, after the tab, where `"os"` starts.

choices.text: Two errors were found on five lines
choices.why: There is one error. `file:line:column` is the shape of every position the toolchain prints.

prompt: A teammate's program compiles, and its log has a line reading `took %!s(int=42) ms`. Which tool would have reported the mistake without running the program?
hint: It reads format strings.

choices.text: `gofmt`, which checks every line
choices.why: `gofmt` changes layout and never reads what a format string asks for.

choices.text: The compiler, which would refuse to build it
choices.why: It did build: to the compiler the format is just a string.

choices.text: `go vet`
choices.why: Right. It checks the verbs of a format string against the arguments, as it did for `%d` and a string.

choices.text: `go doc fmt.Printf`, which lists the verbs
choices.why: Documentation tells you the rule; it does not read your code to see whether you broke it.

prompt: Which of these stop `go build` from producing a binary at all? Choose all that apply.
hint: Separate the compiler's refusals from the other tools' reports.

choices.text: An imported package the file never uses
choices.why: Yes: `"os" imported and not used` was a compile error, exit status 1.

choices.text: A file that `gofmt -l` lists
choices.why: The messy `main.go` compiled before `go fmt` touched it; layout is never a compile error.

choices.text: A local variable declared and never used
choices.why: Yes, the compiler refuses that the same way; lesson 5 shows it.

choices.text: A `Printf` verb that does not match its argument
choices.why: That built and ran, and printed `%!d(string=Ana)`; only `go vet` complained.
